output.statement: For a tuple containing the opposite-sign integer anchors, the anchors must be {-1,1}. Their nonzero rational common neighbors are exactly the nonzero values f(t)=4t(1-t^2)/(1+t^2)^2 for t in Q. Moreover, a set {1,-1,u,-u,v,-v} is a rational D(1) sextuple exactly when u,v,uv belong to C={x in Q: 1+x and 1-x are rational squares}, u,v are nonzero, and u is not v or -v. This gives an exact reduction, not a resolution of the original existence problem.
assumptions: Elements are rational and nonzero, and distinctness is required.
The two integer anchors have opposite signs.
For the symmetric criterion, the proposed elements have the form {1,-1,u,-u,v,-v}.
quantifiers: For every D(1) tuple containing two opposite-sign integer elements, those anchors are {-1,1}.
For every nonzero rational common neighbor x of -1 and 1, there is a rational parameter t with x=f(t), and every rational t gives a common neighbor, possibly zero.
For all rational u,v, the stated conditions are equivalent to {1,-1,u,-u,v,-v} being a D(1) sextuple.
output.proof:
If integer anchors a,b have opposite signs, then ab is an integer at most -1. Since ab+1 is a rational square, it is nonnegative, so ab≥-1 and therefore ab=-1. Thus {a,b}={-1,1}. For any other element x, the anchor-pair conditions make 1+x and 1-x rational squares, hence nonnegative. Therefore -1≤x≤1. Distinctness excludes the endpoints, and the only integer strictly between them is zero, which cannot be an element. In particular, further elements are noninteger rationals in (-1,1); this does not force them to be positive.

For a common neighbor x, choose p,q in Q with p²=1+x and q²=1-x. Then p²+q²=2 and x=p²-1. Because x≠0, p≠1. Set t=(q-1)/(p-1), which is finite. Substituting q=1+t(p-1) into p²+q²=2 and factoring out the base-point solution p=1 gives (1+t²)(p-1)+2(1+t)=0. Since 1+t²≠0 in Q, this yields p=(t²-2t-1)/(t²+1) and q=(1-2t-t²)/(t²+1). Consequently x=p²-1=4t(1-t²)/(1+t²)²=f(t). Conversely, these formulas satisfy p²+q²=2, so x=f(t)=p²-1 has 1+x=p² and 1-x=q². Thus every rational t gives a common neighbor, which may be zero. The conic point (1,-1) not represented by this finite slope also gives x=0, so no nonzero common neighbor is omitted.

Now let C={x in Q:1+x and 1-x are rational squares}. In the proposed symmetric set, the anchor-to-element pairs require u,v in C, and the four cross-pairs between {u,-u} and {v,-v} require uv in C. Conversely, those conditions provide all anchor-to-element and cross-pair squares. The remaining two pairs, (u,-u) and (v,-v), have values 1-u²=(1+u)(1-u) and 1-v²=(1+v)(1-v), also rational squares. The anchor pair has value zero. This accounts for all fifteen pairs. Since ±1 are not in C (one of 1±1 is 2, which is not a rational square), u,v in C prevent collisions with the anchors. Nonzero u,v prevent collisions within each opposite pair, and u≠±v is exactly what prevents collisions between the two pairs. This proves the iff criterion.

By the parametrization, the symmetric condition can equivalently be written u=f(r), v=f(s), uv=f(w) for r,s,w in Q, with f(r), f(s), f(w) nonzero and f(r)≠±f(s). The parameter equation is f(r)f(s)=f(w); clearing denominators gives 4rs(1-r²)(1-s²)(1+w²)² = w(1-w²)(1+r²)²(1+s²)². This is an exact algebraic reduction, but it is a relation in three rational parameters and establishes neither a nondegenerate solution nor an obstruction. The symmetric criterion does not cover general sextuples containing {-1,1}, where the four common neighbors need not occur in opposite pairs.
gaps: The rational solutions of f(r)f(s)=f(w) satisfying the nonzero and distinctness conditions have not been classified; no symmetric nondegenerate sextuple or obstruction is established.
The symmetric paired criterion does not address arbitrary four pairwise adjacent common neighbors of {-1,1}; no obstruction for that general exceptional-anchor case is proved.
The all-positive case cannot contain the exceptional anchors and is not resolved by this argument.
No unbounded-height obstruction or exact witness resolving the original main goal is supplied.
output.method_summary: Reduce opposite-sign integer anchors to {-1,1}, parametrize their common-neighbor conic by the slope of a line through (1,1), and verify all pair conditions for the symmetric candidate by organizing the fifteen pairs into anchor, opposite-pair, and cross-pair classes.

direction_proposals.label: Classify the symmetric parameter relation
direction_proposals.assignment: Study rational solutions of the cleared equation for f(r)f(s)=f(w), treating zero, collision, and other exceptional loci separately; seek either a nondegenerate example or a proved rational-point obstruction.

target_claim.statement: Classify the rational triples (r,s,w) satisfying f(r)f(s)=f(w) with f(r), f(s), f(w) nonzero and f(r)≠±f(s), or prove that no such triple exists.
quantifiers: Over all rational triples (r,s,w), without a height bound.

direction_proposals.assignment: Investigate four distinct pairwise adjacent nonzero rational common neighbors of {-1,1} without assuming opposite-pair symmetry; seek a global obstruction or exact example.

target_claim.statement: Determine whether there exist four distinct nonzero rational common neighbors of {-1,1} that are pairwise adjacent under the relation xy+1 is a rational square.
assumptions: Each neighbor x satisfies 1+x and 1-x are rational squares.
quantifiers: Over all rational neighbors with no height bound and no imposed sign or symmetry conditions.
